summary: Mark Tatz (1946–2021) specialized in Buddhist studies, Tibetology, and Indology. He earned his PhD from the University of British Columbia under Leon Hurvitz in 1978 and also studied under traditional teachers. He is attested as a professor at the California Institute of Integral Studies in 1988.

Mark Teeuwen (born 1966) is a scholar of Japanology and religious studies. He completed his MA (~1984–1989) and PhD (~1990–1996) at Leiden University. He served as a lecturer at Cardiff University (1994–1999) before becoming a professor at the University of Oslo in 1999.

Mark Wilks (1759–1831) worked in the fields of history, archaeology, and Indology. He served as Resident at the Kingdom of Mysore (~1803–1808) and Governor of Saint Helena (~1813–1816), and became a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1826.
Mark William Carr (1833–1871) worked in Indology and linguistics. He served as Assistant Inspector General for the Madras Police in 1862 and held the rank of Major in the Madras Staff Corps in 1870.
Mark Zebrowski (1944–1999) was an Indology and history/archaeology scholar. He studied at Dartmouth College (~1962–1966) and Harvard University (~1966–1970).

Markus Gabriel (born 1980) is a philosopher who studied at the University of Bonn (~2000–2002). He has held posts at Heidelberg University, The New School, the University of Bonn (appointed professor in 2009), The New Institute, Kyoto Institute of Philosophy, and Kyoto University.

Markus Viehbeck works in Tibetology and Buddhist studies. He completed his PhD at the University of Vienna in 2012 under Helmut Tauscher and Franz-Karl Ehrhard. His career includes work as a project researcher at Heidelberg University and a faculty post at the University of Vienna (attested 2026).

Marsha Weidner is a scholar of Sinology, history/archaeology, and Buddhist studies who earned her PhD from the University of California, Berkeley. She held an assistant professorship at the University of Virginia (attested 1990) and a professorship at the University of Kansas (attested 2001).

Marshall Livingston Perrin (1855–1935) was a linguist. He studied at Harvard University (~1870–1874, 1877–1880) and earned his PhD from the University of Göttingen (1883–1889), where he also taught. He later served as assistant professor (1888–1891) and professor of Sanskrit (1910) at Boston University.

Marshall Sahlins (1930–2021) was a history and archaeology scholar who studied at the University of Michigan (~1947–1952) and Columbia University (~1952–1954). He held posts at the University of Michigan (~1957–1973) and the University of Chicago (1973).
Marta Bianco specializes in Sinology and Tibetology. She earned two master's degrees from the University of Naples "L'Orientale" (-2023, -2025) and became a PhD candidate there in 2024.

Marta Sanvido researches religious studies, Japanology, and Buddhist studies. She held posts at Ca' Foscari University of Venice (2019–2020), UC Berkeley (2021–2023), and the University of Hamburg (2023–2024), before becoming an assistant professor at Yale University in 2025.

Marta Sernesi is a scholar of Tibetology and Buddhist studies. She earned her PhD from the University of Turin in 2007 and is attested as a visiting professor (Gastprofessorin) at the Göttingen Academy of Sciences and Humanities in 2026.

Martha A. Muusses (1894–1981) was an Indology and religious studies scholar who earned her PhD from Utrecht University in 1920 under Willem Caland. She worked for the Batavian Society of Arts and Sciences (1921–1926) and taught Dutch at Copenhagen, Stockholm, Uppsala, and Gothenburg.

Martha Ann Selby (born 1954) is an Indologist. She served as series editor for South Asia Research (attested 2014), is a professor emeritus at the University of Texas at Austin (attested 2026), and holds professorships and a department chair at Harvard University (attested 2026).
Martha Lile Love (1950–1979) was a scholar in Indology. She studied at the University of Toronto (~1968–1972) and undertook further studies at Savitribai Phule Pune University.

Martha Nussbaum (born 1947) is a philosopher who studied at Wellesley, NYU, and Harvard, learning under Bernard Williams in 1973. She held academic posts at Oxford, Harvard, Brown, and since 1995 has been a distinguished professor at the University of Chicago.

Martin Baumann (born 1960) works in religious and Buddhist studies. He earned a PhD from Leibniz University Hannover (~1989–1993) and completed his Habilitation at the University of Leipzig (~1994–1999). In 2001, he became a professor at the University of Lucerne.

Martin Brauen (born 1948) works in Tibetology, history/archaeology, and Buddhist studies, having studied under multiple traditional teachers and at the universities of Delhi and Zurich (doctoral degree, ~1976). He held leadership and curatorial posts at the Ethnographic Museum of the University of Zurich and the Rubin Museum of Art.

Martin Collcutt (born 1939) is a scholar of Japanology, history, and Buddhist studies. After studying at Cambridge and Harvard (PhD 1975) and teaching in Japan (1963–1969), he served as East Asian Studies Program Director at Princeton University (1975–2015).
